question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}y=xy+4.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =xy+4 \\ {x}^{2}y-xy & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,2)={f}_{y}(2,2)\,i-{f}_{x}(2,2)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-xy)\,j \\  & =({x}^{2}-x)\,i-(2xy-y)\,j \\ t(2,2) & =({2}^{2}-2)\,i-(2(2)(2)-2)\,j \\  & =2\,i-6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $2\,i-6\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡xy \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(0,\frac{\pi }{2})={f}_{y}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})i-{f}_{x}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\,j \\ t(0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))j \\  & =-i+\frac{\pi }{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-i+\frac{\pi }{2}\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(\frac{\pi }{2},0)={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)i-{f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)j \\  & =(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)j \\ t(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =(-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡0+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))j \\  & =i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}=e-y.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1} & =e-y \\ x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y & =e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,0)={f}_{y}(1,0)i-{f}_{x}(1,0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y)j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+1)i-{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,j \\ t(1,0) & =(2(1)(0){e}^{0+1}+1)i-{e}^{0+1}\,j \\  & =i-e\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-e\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y=8xy+2-8e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =8xy+2-8e \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy & =2-8e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2-8e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)={f}_{y}(1,e)\,i-{f}_{x}(1,e)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{2x}{y}-8x)i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8y)\,j \\ t(1,e) & =(\frac{2(1)}{e}-8(1))i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-8(e))\,j \\  & =(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)j\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, our tangent vector is $(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2xy+9.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2xy+9 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,2)={f}_{y}(-1,2)\,i-{f}_{x}(-1,2)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9)\,j \\  & =(2y-2x)\,i-(2x-2y)\,j \\ t(-1,2) & =(2(2)-2(-1))\,i-(2(-1)-2(2))\,j \\  & =6\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $6\,i+6\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x+1={x}^{2}y.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={x}^{2}y \\ {x}^{2}y-x-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-x-1$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,2)={f}_{y}(1,2)i-{f}_{x}(1,2)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-x-1)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-x-1)j \\  & ={x}^{2}\,i-(2xy-1)j \\ t(1,2) & =(1)^{2}\,i-(2(1)(2)-1)j \\  & =i-3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-3\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}y={y}^{2}+3.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & ={y}^{2}+3 \\ {x}^{2}y-{y}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,1)={f}_{y}(2,1)\,i-{f}_{x}(2,1)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-{y}^{2})\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =({x}^{2}-2y)\,i-2xy\,j \\ t(2,1) & =({2}^{2}-2(1))\,i-2(2)(1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $2\,i-4\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x\operatorname{ln}⁡y={x}^{2}-1.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-{x}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-{x}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,1)={f}_{y}(-1,1)\,i-{f}_{x}(-1,1)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-{x}^{2})\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-{x}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{x}{y}\,i-(\operatorname{ln}⁡y-2x)\,j \\ t(-1,1) & =\frac{(-1)}{1}\,i-(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-2(-1))\,j \\  & =-i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-i-2\,j.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =1-{x}^{2}+2y \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x^{2} - x y - 3 y=5.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-2,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=x^{2} - x y - 3 y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=5.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-2,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-2,-1)=f_y(-2,-1)i-f_x(-2,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^{2} - x y - 3 y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^{2} - x y - 3 y)\,j \\ &=(- x - 3)\,i-(2 x - y)\,j \\ t(-2,-1)&=(- \left(-2\right) - 3)\,i-(2 \left(-2\right) - \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(-1)\,i-(-3)\,j \\ &=-i+3\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-i+3\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)}=-4 - e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-4 - e.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)=f_y(1,e)i-f_x(1,e)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(- x - \frac{3 x}{y})\,i-(- 2 x - y - 3 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(1,e)&=(- \left(1\right) - \frac{3 \left(1\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(- 2 \left(1\right) - \left(e\right) - 3 \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(- \frac{3}{e} - 1)\,i-(-5 - e)\,j \\ &=-\left(1 + \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(e + 5\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-\left(1 + \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(e + 5\right)\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y=0.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,1)=f_y(2,1)i-f_x(2,1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y)\,j \\ &=(4 x + 4)\,i-(- 6 x + 4 y)\,j \\ t(2,1)&=(4 \left(2\right) + 4)\,i-(- 6 \left(2\right) + 4 \left(1\right))\,j \\ &=(12)\,i-(-8)\,j \\ &=12\, i+8\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $12\, i+8\, j.$

\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} - x y + x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} - x y + x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(- x + \frac{x}{y})\,i-(- 6 x - y + \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(-2,e)&=(- \left(-2\right) + \frac{\left(-2\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(- 6 \left(-2\right) - \left(e\right) + \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(2 - \frac{2}{e})\,i-(13 - e)\,j \\ &=\left(2 - \frac{2}{e}\right)\, i-\left(13 - e\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $\left(2 - \frac{2}{e}\right)\, i-\left(13 - e\right)\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)}=12 + 2 e^{2}.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,e^{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=12 + 2 e^{2}.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,e^{2})$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,e^{2})=f_y(2,e^{2})i-f_x(2,e^{2})j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,e^{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(x + \frac{4 x}{y})\,i-(- 2 x + y + 4 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(2,e^{2})&=(\left(2\right) + \frac{4 \left(2\right)}{\left(e^{2}\right)})\,i-(- 2 \left(2\right) + \left(e^{2}\right) + 4 \ln{\left(\left(e^{2}\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(\frac{8}{e^{2}} + 2)\,i-(4 + e^{2})\,j \\ &=\left(\frac{8}{e^{2}} + 2\right)\, i-\left(4 + e^{2}\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $\left(\frac{8}{e^{2}} + 2\right)\, i-\left(4 + e^{2}\right)\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y=-6.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-6.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,-1)=f_y(-1,-1)i-f_x(-1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y)\,j \\ &=(x + 4)\,i-(- 6 x + y)\,j \\ t(-1,-1)&=(\left(-1\right) + 4)\,i-(- 6 \left(-1\right) + \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(3)\,i-(5)\,j \\ &=3\, i-5\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $3\, i-5\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} - x y - y=-1.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} - x y - y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,-1)=f_y(1,-1)i-f_x(1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} - x y - y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} - x y - y)\,j \\ &=(- x - 1)\,i-(- 6 x - y)\,j \\ t(1,-1)&=(- \left(1\right) - 1)\,i-(- 6 \left(1\right) - \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(-2)\,i-(-5)\,j \\ &=-2\, i+5\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-2\, i+5\, j.$
